title: Good zeal (ch. 72)
hook: bear one another's weaknesses of body and character with patience

segments.voice: Yesterday, stability: the monk's promise to stay with one community, in one place. Your line was stay. What did you stay with a little longer than you meant to? Day one thousand two hundred three.

Zeal has a mixed reputation. A zealous fan, a zealous inspector, a zealous neighbor with a clipboard and opinions about your lawn. Fire, yes, but often the kind that burns other people. Near the very end of his Rule, after chapters on prayer, work, food, sleep and punishment, Benedict stops to talk about zeal. He doesn't tell his monks to have less of it. He says there are two kinds, and they lead in opposite directions. Yesterday's promise was to stay with the same brothers for life. Today's chapter answers the obvious next question: how do you live with them? Today: good zeal.
screen: `ZEAL: FIRE THAT CAN BURN.` → `TWO KINDS, TWO DIRECTIONS.` → `HOW DO YOU LIVE WITH THEM?`

segments.voice: Chapter seventy-two is short, and it opens with the contrast. There is a bad zeal of bitterness, Benedict says, which separates a person from God and leads toward hell. And there is a good zeal, which separates a person from vices and leads toward God and everlasting life. Same energy, opposite ends. The bitter kind is the one that keeps a list of everyone else's faults. The good kind, he says, is what monks should practice with the warmest love. Then he spells out what it looks like, and the list is almost entirely about other people. First, they should outdo one another in showing honor. That echoes Saint Paul in the Douay-Rheims: "Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood, with honour preventing one another." Preventing there is an old sense: going ahead of, getting there first. Then comes the line today is built on. They should bear one another's weaknesses, of body or of character, with the greatest patience. Of body: the brother who snores, who's slow, who's sick again. Of character: the brother who interrupts, who sulks, who is exactly as irritating today as he was yesterday. Benedict doesn't say fix them, or report them, or pretend they aren't there. He says bear them. Paul again: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." Next, no one should chase what seems best for himself, but rather what is best for someone else. And the chapter ends with a line that gathers it all up: prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may he bring us all together to everlasting life. All together. Benedict's last picture of heaven includes the snorer.
screen: `A BITTER ZEAL AND A GOOD ZEAL.` · `OUTDO ONE ANOTHER IN HONOR.` · `BEAR WEAKNESS OF BODY AND OF CHARACTER.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · then: `BRING US ALL TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with a flaw. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose habit wears on you. Not a great wrong, just the small, repeated thing. Picture it happening. Notice the bitter zeal rising, the urge to correct or keep score. Then, without excusing anything, just set the weight on your shoulders for a moment and carry it. If it helps, notice one weakness of your own that someone else carries for you. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Good zeal. In Benedict's Rule, the fire that leads away from vice and toward God, and shows itself in honor and patience toward others. Today's word.
Your line: bear with each other. Today, when that habit shows up, let it pass once without a word or a look. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities read the Rule aloud in portions through the year, and chapter seventy-two on good zeal is often cited by monks and oblates as a summary of how to live together.

fork.setup: you live with the same brothers for life, and one of them has a habit that grates on you every single day. what does chapter seventy-two ask?
options: correct him until the habit stops.
keep your distance so it doesn't bother you.
bear it, with the greatest patience.
fork.reveal: Benedict asks monks to bear one another's weaknesses of body or character with the greatest patience, and to outdo one another in honor.

original.note: Latin: good zeal, the subject of chapter seventy-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: zeal means being intense about your cause.
what it means: Benedict names a bitter zeal and a good zeal; the good kind looks like honor and patience toward others.
what a scholar hears: the chapter weaves in Paul's words from Romans 12:10, and closes with 'prefer nothing whatever to Christ.'

notes: The Rule is paraphrased. Check the summary of ch. 72: evil zeal of bitterness separating from God and leading to hell; good zeal separating from vices and leading to God and everlasting life; practiced with most fervent love; anticipate one another in honor (Rom 12:10); bear infirmities of body or character with the greatest patience; vie in obedience; no one following what seems useful for himself but rather for another; 'prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may he bring us all together to life everlasting.'
Galatians 6:2 is not quoted in ch. 72 itself; it is offered alongside as a related text. Confirm that is acceptable, or cut.

'Near the very end of his Rule' and 'chapters on … punishment' (the penal code, chs. 23–30): confirm framing.
